title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Automotive | Dye PT (US)
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for US automotive plants: aluminum castings, stainless parts, tooling repairs and fixtures. Request a PT inspection quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Automotive Plants and Suppliers in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT, dye penetrant inspection) reveals surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps on parts of any non-porous material, including the aluminum die castings and stainless steel components that make up much of a modern vehicle. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to automotive plants and suppliers across the United States to examine castings, machined faces, welded fixtures and tooling repairs, and reports every indication. Request a PT inspection quote to scope the work.

Why penetrant testing matters in automotive manufacturing

Vehicles are increasingly built from aluminum, stainless alloys and non-ferrous castings chosen to save weight and resist corrosion, and none of those can be magnetized. Penetrant testing is the surface method that works on them. It also works on ferromagnetic parts where a magnetic method is impractical, such as a small machined feature, a recess that the yoke cannot reach, or a coated surface that only needs a pinhole check. Cracks, cold shuts and porosity that reach the surface of a die casting are exactly what the method is built to show.

The method needs a surface that is open: a flaw filled with oil, machining smear or paint will not take up penetrant. That makes pre-cleaning a technical step, not a formality, and much of the quality of a penetrant examination is decided before the liquid is applied.

Parts and assets we examine

  • Aluminum castings: engine and transmission housings, brackets and structural castings, examined at machined faces, sealing surfaces and thin-wall regions where porosity or cracks leak or fatigue. See penetrant testing of castings for the casting-specific method.
  • Stainless and nickel alloy components: exhaust parts, manifolds and turbocharger housings, and the welds that join them.
  • Tooling repairs: die inserts and cores where a crack was ground out and repaired by welding; the excavation and the finished repair are both examined.
  • Weld fixtures and robot cells: aluminum and stainless fixture components, and locations where magnetic particle yokes will not fit.
  • Machined sealing faces and threaded features: surfaces where a hairline crack becomes a leak path after assembly.

Standards and the plant's own system

As in other automotive inspection, the plant's quality system, typically built on IATF 16949 with customer-specific requirements, governs records and containment. That system is the plant's, not ours. We follow your procedure or a written one we prepare for you, and we report in a format that fits your control plan.

Technical references include ASTM E165 for penetrant examination of general industrial parts, ASTM E1417 for the process specification for penetrant systems, ASTM E433 for reference photographs of casting indications, MSS SP-93 for castings and forgings in valves and fittings, and ASME Section V Article 6 for code work. Our explanation of ASME Section V Article 6 gives the background. Acceptance limits come from the purchase specification, drawing or customer requirement; we apply the supplied limits and the plant decides.

Technique details for castings and machined surfaces

  • System choice: water-washable fluorescent systems handle the rough surfaces of as-cast parts; solvent-removable visible systems suit field repairs and fixtures; post-emulsified fluorescent systems are chosen where the specification demands the highest sensitivity.
  • Pre-cleaning: die-casting release agents, machining coolant and oil must be removed with an approved cleaner. Shot blasting or machining can smear aluminum over a crack, closing it; an etch or longer cleaning cycle may be required afterward.
  • Temperature: the usual window under ASME Section V Article 6 runs from about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; plants and yards in cold or hot weather need a procedure that covers the real temperature.
  • Dwell and removal: dwell time depends on the alloy and the flaw type. Over-washing removes penetrant from shallow flaws, under-washing leaves background that hides indications.
  • Developer and viewing: a thin even developer coat, evaluated within the time the procedure allows, in white light or in ultraviolet light measured at the part.
  • Chemistry limits: parts that go into stainless or nickel assemblies may need penetrant materials with controlled halogen and sulfur content, and the report records the batch.

What PT finds and what it misses in automotive work

PT shows surface cracks, shrinkage that reaches a machined face, cold shuts, laps and weld defects open to the surface. It compares poorly with other methods in three situations: where the flaw is below the surface, where a rough or smeared surface seals the opening, and where the part is porous, so that penetrant bleeds out of the material itself. A porous casting that has not been impregnated can give a flooded background and make fine indications impossible to read. When the question is internal soundness of a casting, ultrasonic testing for automotive plants is the method to ask about, and for steel parts magnetic particle inspection for automotive plants is often faster.

What the PT report contains

Typical contents of an automotive PT report
ItemWhat we record
Part or assetPlant, line or die number, part number, alloy, lot or heat where known, and surface condition
ProcedureProcedure and revision, specification and edition, acceptance criterion
MaterialsPenetrant family, remover, developer, manufacturer and batch numbers
Process controlPart temperature, pre-cleaning method, dwell and developer times
PersonnelTechnician and level under the written practice, with the Level III approving the procedure
FindingsLocation, length and type of each indication, accept or reject, and a marked sketch or photograph

Porosity, impregnation and leak paths

Many automotive castings are pressure-tight parts, such as transmission cases, coolant housings and intake components, and a surface-breaking crack or a line of connected porosity becomes a leak after assembly. Penetrant testing at machined sealing faces is therefore less about structure than about function: does a path exist from one side to the other. An impregnated casting is sealed with a resin after machining, and examination before impregnation shows more about the casting than after. If the plant impregnates, tell us the sequence so the examination is placed where it is meaningful.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

Not every mark that shows is a flaw. A rough as-cast surface holds penetrant in its texture, a machining mark retains liquid, and the edge of a part bleeds out around fasteners or sharp corners. A technician separates these from real indications by the shape of the mark, by how it behaves as developer dries and by wiping and re-examining the spot when the procedure allows. Linear marks, rounded marks and clusters are evaluated against different limits, and the report states which category each indication was placed in. Because interpretation matters as much as application, the procedure names the viewing conditions and the time window.

Two points save plants rework. First, the examination should come after machining and before final cleaning or coating, not after, since anything that smears or fills the surface hides flaws. Second, repeated indications at one location across many parts usually point to a tooling or process cause, such as a die radius or a gate position, and a trend in our reports can help the plant's engineers find it.

What to send for a quote

  • Parts list with drawings, alloy and the surfaces to be examined
  • Specification, acceptance criterion and any customer-specific requirement
  • Quantity and sampling plan for supplier lots, or a full list for repairs and fixtures
  • Release agents, coolants or coatings on the surface, and who pre-cleans
  • Fluorescent or visible requirement, chemistry limits on materials, and darkened-area availability
  • Temperature range at the examination location, lock-out and access details
  • Dates, badging and the site address

Planning in an automotive plant

Penetrant examination is a sequence with waiting built in, so it is planned like a process, not a spot check. On shutdown work the sequence runs surface preparation, penetrant application, dwell, removal, developer, interpretation and post-cleaning, and tooling rarely sits idle long enough to allow the sequence twice. Parts that must go back into production after repair need a post-clean that removes developer residue, and the plant's cleanliness rules decide how. Solvent-based materials are flammable, so hot-work rules and ventilation apply on the plant floor.

At a supplier, penetrant examination fits where lots are held for release. Temperature is the item most often forgotten in plants with open dock doors or heated enclosures that fall below the standard range after the second shift ends. Procedure development and demonstration are available through NDT technical procedure development.

Training plant technicians

If you prefer to run penetrant testing yourself, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training are the starting point, and the penetrant testing simulator provides practice without consuming materials. The employer issues the qualification under its written practice. See also NDT training for manufacturing.

Boundaries of this service

Atlantis does not take on radiography in the United States, where it is a licensed activity, and the specialist methods are not offered on this page. We do not release product, impregnate castings or repair parts. Penetrant testing finds only flaws open to the surface. More background is in penetrant testing and MT versus PT.

faq.q: Can PT be used on porous aluminum die castings?
faq.a: It can, but porosity at the surface can flood the background and hide fine indications. Impregnated castings give cleaner results. We note surface porosity on the report so the plant can judge whether the examination is meaningful for that part.

faq.q: Why do you ask what release agent or coolant is on the part?
faq.a: Die-casting release agents and machining coolant fill surface flaws and block penetrant. The cleaning method depends on what is on the surface, and an approved cleaner is part of the procedure, so we need to know before mobilizing.

faq.q: What do you need to quote PT for an automotive plant?
faq.a: Send the parts list with drawings and alloy, the specification and acceptance criterion, quantities or sampling plan, surface condition and coatings, fluorescent or visible requirement, any chemistry limits, temperature at the location, dates and site address.

faq.q: Is PT or MT better for tooling repairs?
faq.a: On steel dies MT is faster, but PT is appropriate when the repair area is small, recessed or coated, or when the tool material is non-magnetic. The excavation and the finished weld are both examined, and the choice follows the part.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: The purchase specification, drawing or customer requirement sets the limits, and the plant's quality organization or the customer makes the disposition. Our report classifies and locates every indication so the decision is straightforward.

faq.q: Do you work at the supplier or at our assembly plant?
faq.a: Both. Technicians travel to the foundry, machining plant or assembly plant, examine the parts there and report. Scope, sampling and reporting format are agreed with you before the crew travels to the site.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard window of about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Plants with cold docks or hot process areas need a procedure that covers the actual conditions, and we confirm this at quotation.

faq.q: Can you examine stainless exhaust components without contaminating them?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant materials with controlled halogen and sulfur content are available, and we record batch numbers on the report. Tell us the chemistry limit your specification sets so the right materials are on the job.

No. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer qualifies its own personnel. Our Level II technicians perform and interpret under Atlantis's written practice, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.
